Q60761235.summary: Carved in marble, a youthful shepherd with thick curls stands calmly with a large sheep across his shoulders, his cloak hanging over one arm and his crook beside him, while small sheep rest at his feet beside a tree stump. Found together with a set of statuettes telling the story of Jonah, the figure almost certainly represents Christ as the Good Shepherd, a serene image of protection and hope for the afterlife.
facts: It belongs to a group of small marble sculptures in Cleveland (1965.237–247), including four Jonah statuettes; an unconfirmed report says the whole group was found in a single large storage jar (pithos).
The statuette is about 49.5 cm high and is dated c. 280–290, which places it among the earliest surviving sculptures of the Good Shepherd understood as Christ.
The Cleveland Museum of Art acquired it in 1965 through the John L. Severance Fund.

cur:catacombs-columnar-sarcophagus-31499.summary: In one arched niche of a columnar sarcophagus, the young Christ, his hair falling to his shoulders, stands between two bearded apostles who hold out loaves and fish; baskets of bread stand at their feet. The calm, classical carving of the later 4th century gives the miracle the solemnity of a liturgical offering.
facts: Commons dates the sarcophagus to about 350–375; this image shows a detail of its front.
The beardless, long-haired Christ is typical of Theodosian-era sculpture.

cur:catacombs2-ravenna-barbatian-sarcoph.summary: Eight columns divide the front into five niches: vases sprouting plants fill the outer ones, while in the three central niches Christ stands blessing with an open book, between Paul holding a book and Peter carrying the cross. The rigid, frontal figures speak of the solemn court art of late fifth-century Ravenna. On the lid a wreath encloses the monogram of Christ with alpha and omega between two crosses.
facts: It came from the old church of San Lorenzo in Cesarea, between Ravenna and Classe, and in 1658 received the relics of Saint Barbatian, traditionally the confessor of Galla Placidia.
Its back, only roughly carved, shows two lambs facing the Christogram; each short side has a three-legged candlestick.
Italian Wikipedia compares the stiffness of its figures with those of the sarcophagus of Saint Exuperantius in the same cathedral.

cur:manuscripts-augustine-gospels-passio.summary: Twelve small panels in a jewelled frame tell the Passion from Palm Sunday onward: Christ rides into Jerusalem to the cry 'Osanna filio David', presides at the Last Supper over a round table with a chalice, prays on the Mount of Olives, washes the disciples' feet beneath a great lampstand, and is betrayed by Judas's kiss; later panels show Peter's sword drawn in the garden, Christ led before his judges, Pilate washing his hands and the cross carried to Golgotha. Brief Latin captions name several scenes. It is the oldest surviving narrative cycle of the Passion in a Latin Gospel book.
facts: The St Augustine Gospels is the oldest surviving illustrated Latin Gospel book; tradition holds that it was brought to England by St Augustine's mission in 597 or sent to him by Pope Gregory the Great in 601.
Only two picture pages survive — this one and the portrait of Luke — giving 24 small scenes from Christ's life, a very rare survival from the old Western Empire.
The manuscript is still used for the oath at the enthronement of each new Archbishop of Canterbury, and in 2023 it was carried in the coronation procession of King Charles III.
cur:manuscripts-augustine-gospels-passio.notes: Captions were partly added in England in the late 7th or 8th century (per Wikipedia). Identification of each of the lower-row scenes follows the captions where legible.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-8-christ-.summary: Supported by four angels and flanked by six more bearing cross-staffs, the Christ-Logos sits in a round mandorla high in the heavens as the psalmist addresses him with outstretched hands. Beneath him a group of 'babes and sucklings' sing his praise, while an angel drives demons into a pit and the moon, stars, birds and fish of the psalm fill the scene. It is the psalm Christ himself quoted at his entry into Jerusalem.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-8-christ-.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-66-christ.summary: From a rock the psalmist addresses the cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, who leans out of heaven holding a pair of scales and blessing his people with his right hand: 'God be merciful unto us, and bless us'. At the left the nations of the earth wait to be judged, and at the right the earth's increase appears as a tree, vines and grain. It is a short, serene drawing for a psalm of blessing.

cur:manuscripts2-escorial-lamb-on-mount-.summary: A white Lamb marked with a cross stands on the mountain at the centre of the page, surrounded by rows of the redeemed and by figures with harps, while above, an angel and figures look on. The scene illustrates John's vision, 'I looked, and, lo, a Lamb stood on the mount Sion, and with him an hundred forty and four thousand'. Here the Lamb is Christ, worshipped by those who 'follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth'.
facts: The Escorial Beatus has 151 surviving leaves and 52 miniatures; it was probably made at San Millán de la Cogolla and was already in the Escorial library in the 16th century.
Its figures, with huge eyes and boldly patterned drapery, are among the most expressive in the Beatus tradition.

cur:monumental-faras-virgin-and-child.summary: The Virgin, robed in deep red with a large golden halo, gazes out with wide, dark-outlined eyes, raising one hand while holding the small Christ Child at her shoulder. Though the surface is badly abraded, the strong outlines and warm earth colours are characteristic of the earliest phase of painting at Faras.
facts: Faras (ancient Pachoras), a major city of Christian Nubia, was flooded by Lake Nasser in the 1960s; before that, a Polish team led by Kazimierz Michałowski excavated its cathedral (1960–64) during UNESCO's Nubian salvage campaign, and the paintings were divided between Khartoum and Warsaw.
The Warsaw museum dates this painting to the 8th or first half of the 9th century, among the earlier layers of the cathedral's decoration.

cur:monumental2-bawit-room-30-virgin-and.summary: In this detail from a niche painting, the Virgin, with large dark eyes and a halo, looks out frontally from her throne, holding the small Christ Child before her breast; the Greek abbreviations for 'Mother of God' flank her head. The direct, wide-eyed gaze is typical of the icon-like monastic paintings of Bawit.
facts: The slide's handwritten label identifies the painting as the Virgin in the niche of Room 30 ('Baouit. Salle 30. Niche de la Vierge, détail').
Enthroned Virgins with the Child were frequent in the prayer niches of the monks' cells at Bawit and Saqqara.
cur:monumental2-bawit-room-30-virgin-and.notes: Historical photograph (EuroPhot glass slide); an overall view of the niche is also on Commons (GDE000855).

cur:monumental2-san-vincenzo-christ-betw.summary: In the conch of a small apse, Christ stands frontally on a deep blue ground, haloed and holding a jewelled Gospel book, blessing in the Greek manner; the two deacon-martyrs Lawrence and Stephen, in light robes, turn towards him from either side. The image crowns a crypt whose walls also show the martyrdoms of these two saints.
facts: The crypt was painted for Abbot Epiphanius (824–842), who appears as a kneeling donor beside the Crucifixion on another wall of the same small chamber.
Lawrence and Stephen, both deacons and early martyrs, were often paired in Roman and Benedictine devotion.
